short_answer: Joe Duffy runs a real, long running pick business. OffshoreInsiders.com lists a mailing address in Alpharetta, Georgia, an email address, a published price for every package and the date each one runs to. Payment goes through PayPal, which also takes cards. In that narrow sense it is legitimate.

Whether his picks make money is not shown on his own site. It claims he has "the most units won of all time" and that over any long period he will hit "near or above the 60 percentile," but it publishes no record, and its FAQ says "it would not be wise to advertise losing days."

The numbers we could check come from marketplaces that sell his picks. On 20 Nov 2026 the SportsCapping season board had him 20th by profit at 722-673-18 for 2026, a 51.8% win rate and a 0.5% return on flat $100 bets. StatsAlt showed 84-79-1 and +2.00 units. CappersPicks showed a better college football stretch, 47-37 over 60 days. None of these is close to 60%, and all of them are kept by companies that earn money when his picks sell.

Buyer feedback is very thin. The only first hand complaint we found is a 2012 Sportsbook Review post from someone who bought a month of a different OffshoreInsiders service and said they lost over $2,000. Treat Duffy as an experienced seller whose marketing goes far beyond the numbers we found. If you buy, start with a day or a week, record every pick with the line you got, and judge it after a few hundred picks.

guarantee: OffshoreInsiders does not sell a guarantee. Its FAQ answers "Why not guarantee your picks like some other sites?" at length, says "Anyone who wants a guarantee frankly should not be gambling," and states: "we do not give refunds for occasional losing days." Packages run on consecutive days, like a newspaper subscription, with exceptions only for some monthly or longer buyers.

The FAQ argues that guarantees elsewhere are a gimmick: it says sellers who guarantee a winning day release an odd number of plays so they need a lower hit rate, and that make good days are used by services that "charge 20 times what we do." That is a fair point about how many guarantees work, and it is also a reason this site gives nothing back after a bad run.

There is a twist. The OffshoreInsiders page announcing its sister site, PicksDepot.com, says PicksDepot gives bettors "guaranteed selections" while OffshoreInsiders offers "lower-priced, non-guaranteed packages." We did not find PicksDepot's guarantee terms, so we cannot say whether that means cash, credit or more picks.

The FAQ also has no refund wording for a double charge or a failed delivery. It tells buyers with an "already paid" error to reload or change browser, and to use the contact form for account problems, because phone support was dropped.

claims_note: How we checked: OffshoreInsiders posts no record, so we used the boards of the marketplaces that sell his picks. SportsCapping's season board for 2026 (1 Jan to 20 Nov, flat $100 bets) listed him at 722 wins, 673 losses and 18 pushes, $759 profit and a 0.5% return. 722 divided by 1,395 decided picks is 51.8%. At the average odds these boards show for him, about -106, a bettor needs roughly 51.5% to break even, so this is close to flat. To reach the 60% the FAQ promises, he would have needed about 837 wins out of those 1,395 decisions, 115 more than he had.

We also compared two dates. On 7 Nov 2026 the same board showed him at 686-638 with $923 profit. By 20 Nov it was 722-673 with $759. That means the 13 days in between went about 36-35 and lost about $164 on $100 bets. Short stretches like this mean little alone, but they show the record is moving sideways, not toward 60%.

The biggest claims come with no numbers at all. "The most units won of all time" names no total, no period and no source. The FAQ is unusually frank about why: asked why the site never talks about losers, it compares itself to restaurants that do not post bad reviews and says "it would not be wise to advertise losing days," while promising "There will be no inaccurate records posted." What you see on the site is chosen to sell.

The biographies disagree with each other. OffshoreInsiders and a 2016 press release say full time since 1988, while a StatsAlt pick listing on 20 Nov 2026 said "professionally since 1985." One bio says a winning March Madness every year since 1998, another says since 1988. None of this proves anything about results, but it is a reason to treat the career claims as marketing copy.
record: What a buyer can check outside OffshoreInsiders: three marketplaces that sell his picks publish numbers. SportsCapping's 2026 season board had him at 722-673-18, 51.8%, $759 profit and 0.5% return on 20 Nov 2026, ranked 20th of the 31 handicappers shown. StatsAlt showed 84-79-1, 51.53%, +2.00 units and +$200 profit, without naming the period. CappersPicks showed 47-37 and +$627 in college football over the past 60 days. These sites earn money when his picks sell, and we could not open the full pick logs behind any of them, so they are third party figures, not audits.

PicksDepot, the sister site OffshoreInsiders launched, shows a leaderboard with the same top rows and the same "Sc Score" column as SportsCapping, so it appears to draw on the same grading system rather than a separate one. Its leaderboard page says "Joe Duffy is the industry standard," yet he did not appear in the top five rows it displayed.

What is the seller's own marketing: every claim on OffshoreInsiders.com, from "most units won of all time" to the 60% target. The site has no results page we could find. Its FAQ says it is not set up to post plays after they start, criticises other sites for grading at the best line ever available, and says it grades its own plays strictly, but it does not publish those grades.
We found no court or regulator action involving Joe Duffy or OffshoreInsiders in our searches, and the Better Business Bureau returned no business profile for OffshoreInsiders.

our_data.text: Watchdog grades picks captured from public posts before the game starts. In this edition Joe Duffy is not matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how his picks perform.

customers_intro: Independent buyer evidence on Joe Duffy is very thin for a seller this old. We searched TheRX, Sportsbook Review, Covers, our saved library of Reddit and forum posts, CapperTek reviews and the BBB. Most mentions are reposted plays or the company's own promotion. Below is everything we found and how much weight it can carry. Unhappy buyers are the likeliest to write, so this shows what has gone wrong for some buyers, not how many.

customers.text: We found four buyer related posts over 14 years, all on forums. One is negative: in 2012 a Sportsbook Review member said a month of an OffshoreInsiders service cost them over $2,000 in bets and that the ads showed only the wins. Two are neutral: a 2014 TheRX member who bought and reposted his plays without reporting results, and a 2022 TheRX member who asked if anyone had used him and got no answer. On Reddit we found only the company's own promotional posts. There are no reviews on CapperTek, no BBB profile and no App Store app. Nobody, positive or negative, posted a tracked record of his picks.

In a Sportsbook Review thread warning about pick sellers, a member said they bought a month of a service called "GodsTips" from OffshoreInsiders, lost over $2,000 following it, and that bets were often lost by halftime. They objected that the ads showed a single win without saying the day went 1-6 or worse. The post names an OffshoreInsiders service, not necessarily Duffy's own plays, and gives no full record.
On TheRX forum, a member asked whether anyone had used Joe Duffy and OffshoreInsiders and how the picks were. The replies we read on that page did not answer them.

In a TheRX service plays thread, a member posted the day's Joe Duffy Wise Guy and major plays and wrote that they were "Paid and confirmed by me," which shows they bought them. They did not report how the plays did.
The Reddit posts we found that name OffshoreInsiders, in r/sportsbetting from 2020 and 2021, were written to promote the site and its podcast, not by buyers. We found no Reddit buyer review.

CapperTek's review page for OffshoreInsiders said there were no reviews, and a Better Business Bureau search returned no matching business. On 7 Nov 2026 SmartCustomer (formerly SiteJabber) showed 0 reviews and Trustpilot had no page for offshoreinsiders.com.

conflicts: The OffshoreInsiders homepage carries a MyBookie banner served through an affiliate tracking link (on 7 Nov 2026 the link also carried the promo code MB50), and its article list includes reviews of MyBookie, BetOnline and Bovada. The joeduffy.net blog adds a GT Bets review. Affiliate deals like these usually pay the referrer when readers sign up or lose. Offshore sportsbooks are not licensed by U.S. state regulators, so check the law where you live.

PicksDepot, which says "Joe Duffy is the industry standard," is OffshoreInsiders' own sister site. StatsAlt, SportsCapping, CappersPicks and CapperTek all sell picks too. None of them is a neutral auditor.

The FAQ says the business was built by recruiting "tipsters who have winners to brag about" and that admitting losers "was not a criterion." That tells you the site's selection test is marketing, not a verified record.
strengths: Every package price is published, with the exact date each package runs to, and the cheapest is $21 for a day.
A mailing address and email are listed, and card payment goes through PayPal, so card details are not stored on his site.
The FAQ is blunt that there is no guarantee and no refund, so a buyer knows the terms before paying.
His picks are graded on outside marketplaces, and the numbers there show a roughly break even 2026 rather than heavy losses.
Free picks and long write ups on his blog and podcast let a reader see his method before paying.
concerns: No record on his own site, and an FAQ that says losing days are not advertised.
"Most units won of all time" and the 60% target have no figures behind them; every outside number we found was near 52%.
No refunds, no phone support, and Western Union offered as a payment route for long term buys.
The homepage and blog carry offshore sportsbook affiliate links and promo codes.
Bios on different sites give different start years, 1985 or 1988, and different March Madness streak years.
Almost no independent buyer feedback exists, and the one first hand complaint we found is negative.
checklist: Ask for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Compare the same handicapper across sites. His 2026 numbers on SportsCapping are a better guide than any line on OffshoreInsiders.
Count units, not wins. A 60% record at heavy favorites can still lose money, and 52% at -110 loses.
Pay by card through PayPal rather than Western Union, so you keep a dispute route.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get.
Give any handicapper a few hundred picks before you call them a winner. Short runs swing hard both ways.
faq: OffshoreInsiders is a real, long running business with a mailing address, published prices and PayPal checkout. We could not verify his big claims, such as the most units won of all time, because his site publishes no record, and the outside boards we checked show him close to break even in 2026.
How much does Joe Duffy cost?

On 20 Nov 2026 OffshoreInsiders charged $21 for one day, $39 for two days, $129 for a week, $299 for a month, $899 for 100 days and $1,249 for a year, with no refunds for losing days. Single plays on StatsAlt cost $25.
Does Joe Duffy have a verified record?

Not a full one. SportsCapping showed 722-673-18 with a 0.5% return for 2026, StatsAlt showed 84-79-1, and CappersPicks showed 47-37 in college football over 60 days. These sites sell his picks and we could not open the logs behind them. Watchdog has no graded record for him.

Not on any board we found. His FAQ promises near or above 60% over time, but his 2026 season on SportsCapping is 51.8% and StatsAlt shows 51.5%. Only a 60 day college football slice on CappersPicks was higher, at 56%.
No. The FAQ says it does not give refunds for losing days and argues that guarantees are a gimmick. Its sister site PicksDepot says it sells guaranteed packages, but we did not find those terms.

For $21 a day you get every play he releases from a handicapper active for decades, which is cheap by industry standards. What is unproven is the edge: the outside numbers are close to the 52.4% needed at -110, so after the price of the picks and the lines you can get, a buyer could easily end up behind.
